claim: Australia's war on a cactus ended with a hall named after a moth.

start.title: Cactus
start.description: Family of mostly succulent plants, adapted to dry environments

knots.passage: In Australia, species of Opuntia, particularly Opuntia stricta, were introduced in the 19th century for use as natural agricultural fences and in an attempt to establish a cochineal industry. They rapidly became a major weed problem, but are now controlled by biological agents, particularly the moth Cactoblastis cactorum.
knots.hatnote: Australia imported cacti for a red dye. It got something else.

knots.passage: In some locations, it has spread uncontrollably and was consequently classified an invasive species. However, in other places such as Australia, it has gained favor for its role in the biological control of cacti from the genus Opuntia, such as prickly pear.
knots.hatnote: A pest in some countries, a hero in one.

knots.passage: Prickly pears (mostly Opuntia stricta) were imported into Australia in the First Fleet as hosts of cochineal insects, used in the dye industry. Many of these, especially the tiger pear, quickly became widespread invasive species, rendering 40,000 km (15,000 mi) of farming land unproductive. The moth Cactoblastis cactorum from Argentina, whose larvae eat prickly pear, was introduced in 1925 and almost wiped out the prickly pear. This case is often cited as an example of successful biological pest control.
knots.hatnote: The cactus came with the very first fleet of settlers, and spread.

knots.passage: A monument to Cactoblastis cactorum was erected in Dalby, Queensland, commemorating the eradication of the prickly pear in the region. The Cactoblastis Memorial Hall in Boonarga, Queensland, also commemorates the eradication.
knots.hatnote: Australians did not just thank the moth. They built it things.

knots.passage: In 1925, 3000 cactoblastis eggs were imported from South America. These eggs were divided between the Sherwood laboratory, and the Chinchilla Field Station which had been established in 1923 as one of four Queensland field stations responsible for rearing and distributing insect supplies. The first prickly pear plant was destroyed by the cactoblastis moth at Chinchilla in September 1926. The last extensive area of prickly pear in Queensland was destroyed in 1933, and the Chinchilla Field Station was closed at the end of 1936.
knots.hatnote: Then came the caterpillars, starting from a few thousand eggs.

knots.passage: Proposals to erect a hall at Boonarga were first discussed in July 1934, at which time a public meeting was held and a Hall Committee appointed. Land for the proposed hall was donated by Mrs Fahey, a resident of Boonarga. In October 1934 the Committee decided to name the hall the Boonarga Cactoblastis Memorial Hall in honour of the cactoblastis moth.
knots.hatnote: So the town did the natural thing.

payoff: Prickly pear smothered vast farmlands; moth eggs from South America cleared it within a decade, and a Queensland town named its hall in thanks.
caveats: The moth is now itself an invasive threat to native cacti in the Americas.
